variants.headline: Most of our cities now keep {{majorityFaith}}
body: {{majorityFaith}} now leads in most of our cities, though this nation founded {{founded}}. At a shrine in one town, the keeper still lights the lamp at dawn; by midday the crowd has gone to hear {{majorityFaith}} preached in the square. Nobody has taken the old building away; the people simply walk to a different door.

variants.headline: Keep the faith we founded
body: Neighbors, look into the shops on your own street: {{majorityFaith}} now leads in most of our cities, and the faith we founded, {{founded}}, no longer leads. A child learns the newer songs before she learns the older prayers, and before another generation the older prayers will need teachers. Teach them at home, starting tonight, and do not leave the faith of this nation to hired halls.

variants.headline: My daughter still comes on washing day
body: Sir, your account of {{majorityFaith}} leading in most of our cities reads as though a door had closed. In my house the door stays open: my daughter keeps {{majorityFaith}}, I keep {{founded}}, and the kettle serves both. She still comes round on washing day, and a nation is not poorer for having two prayers at one table.

variants.headline: Who keeps the old shrine open?
body: The interesting question in the shift to {{majorityFaith}} is not which creed leads but who will keep the old prayers alive. In one city, the newer congregation now fills a rented hall, while the shrine of {{founded}} opens to a few quiet families. A faith can lose its majority and still hold the words that made it.

variants.headline: {{city}} takes the faith we founded
body: {{city}} now keeps {{religion}}, the faith this nation founded, as its majority creed. The city's own people made the change, and the shrine there has begun to use the prayers we sing at home. It lies farther from our borders than the towns we call neighbors, which makes the news both stranger and better.

variants.headline: {{cityState}} receives the faith we founded
body: We are informed from {{cityState}} that {{religion}}, the creed this nation founded, now holds a majority in that city. The account describes lamps set in the windows on the eve of the change and a procession that circled the old altars without disturbing them. A shared faith gives our envoys and theirs one subject on which they may speak without quarrel.

variants.headline: Lamps in the windows at {{city}}
body: A carter who hauls salt through {{city}} says the innkeeper now sets lamps in the windows and asks a blessing before she puts down the pot. The city keeps {{religion}}, the creed we founded, and the blessing is one our grandmothers would know. By the second night, other drivers asked him to say it too.

variants.headline: Our faith just took a whole city-state
body: {{city}} now calls {{religion}} its majority faith. It is a city-state on the far side of our neighbors, and its own people carried the creed across. Our faith got there before our traders did. Send the traders.

variants.headline: Our faith reaches {{cityName}}
body: {{cityName}}, a city of {{civilization}} about {{distance}} from our nearest town, now keeps {{religion}}, the faith this nation founded. The change came through the city's own people, and on a weekday the shrine there was busy with families who had brought their washing to the courtyard well. A creed that crosses that many leagues by itself has found hearers we have never met.

variants.headline: A far city takes up our faith
body: A city far beyond our borders now keeps {{religion}}, the faith this nation founded. Travelers describe a shrine beside the road where drivers stop to water their animals, and the keeper there knows the prayers by heart. We cannot say which road will carry the news next.

variants.headline: Our creed gains a distant majority
body: {{cityName}} has become a majority city for {{religion}} in {{civilization}}, a gain for our creed inside another power's lands. It sits {{distance}} from the nearest of our own cities, well beyond the towns we call neighbors.

That is a foothold won by preachers rather than soldiers. A shrine teaching our prayers can shape how a town sees us long after the sermon ends. The question is whether we can keep the friendship of those worshippers without making an enemy of their ruler.

variants.headline: They sing of a far city keeping our faith
body: They tell it at the well: a city {{distance}} from the last market we know has taken up {{religion}}, the faith of our own hearths. The road there is long enough that a song must be shortened to carry. The singers have made a new verse for it, and the verse is ours.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} deepens its faith
body: A household in {{civilization}} has set a new reading beside its door and recites it after the evening meal. The faith of {{religion}} has taken a new form in that country, and the change will reach every town that keeps it. The family learned the words from a traveler and taught them to the neighbors before the week was out.

variants.headline: A foreign power deepens its faith
body: Word comes from a major power abroad that {{religion}} has been deepened. In one town there, a schoolmaster has copied the new words onto a board and hung it where carters can read them. How the older congregations there will receive the change is not yet known.

variants.headline: A creed reformed in a foreign land
body: In this year the people of {{civilization}} reformed the faith of {{religion}}. The elders of that nation set the old books before them, kept the rites they judged sound, and laid the rest aside. A reform is soon done and long remembered, for every household must learn again what it thought it knew.

variants.headline: Notice to readers of divinity
body: Notice is given that {{civilization}} has added to the faith of {{religion}}. The new articles are read at the temples there and will govern the coming feasts. Readers who mean to dispute them should study the text; the informed objection is the one worth printing.

variants.headline: Our faith takes most cities of {{civilization}}
body: {{religion}}, the faith we founded, now leads in most cities of {{civilization}}. In the capital there, a scribe has begun copying our prayers for sale and cannot keep up with the orders. The change happened among the people of that country, one congregation at a time.

variants.headline: Our faith gains ground abroad
body: {{religion}}, the faith founded here, has become the majority in most cities of another major power. Its prayers are now copied and sold in a market we have never seen. The creed has done what no envoy of ours could: it has found a hearing in a distant country.

variants.headline: Will pilgrims from {{civilization}} visit our shrines?
body: The news that {{religion}} now leads in most cities of {{civilization}} is worth more than a good feeling. Worshippers who share our prayers have a reason to visit our shrines, and visitors spend coin at inns and stalls along the way. The trade will follow only if the roads stay open and the welcome stays warm; that is a question for our councils, not our priests.

variants.headline: A potter's bowls for {{civilization}}
variants.byline: A Trader of the Long Roads
body: Sir, I carry salt and cloth into {{civilization}}, and on my last trip the drivers asked me for prayer books more often than for either. Since {{religion}} now leads in most of their cities, that trade will only grow. If your readers know a binder with copies to spare, or a potter with bowls to spare, send them to me before the roads close.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} founds a religion
body: A new faith called {{religion}} has been founded in {{civilization}}. Its first meeting place was a courtyard with a borrowed lamp, and the first speaker read the new words twice because the crowd at the gate kept growing. The creed is young, but it already has a name people will carry to other towns.

variants.headline: A new religion is founded abroad
body: A major power abroad has founded a faith and given it the name {{religion}}. Word reaches us of a first altar raised in a walled garden, where neighbors brought oil and stayed until dark to hear the teaching. Nobody here can say yet how far it will spread.

variants.headline: Entered in the record: a new creed
body: Founder of the creed: {{civilization}}
Name given it: {{religion}}
Seat of the first shrine: {{holyCity}}
One founder, one name, one seat: the account is complete for this year.

variants.headline: A new creed is on the map
body: A new faith has a name tonight: {{religion}}. It was founded in {{civilization}}, and its first shrine is already drawing a crowd. Faiths travel with the people who keep them. Watch the roads, and watch who walks them.

variants.headline: {{religion}} overtakes {{former}} in most of our cities
body: {{religion}} is now the majority faith in most of our cities, taking the lead {{former}} held at the last count. In one market town, the two congregations share a burying ground and argue only about which prayers are said at the gate. The change is a tally in the record; the argument is what the neighbors will remember.

variants.headline: {{religion}} now leads in most of our cities
body: Our cities went without a common majority at the last count. They have one now, and it is {{religion}}. The feast that followed filled the square, and shopkeepers closed early rather than shout over the singing.

variants.headline: Hear it! Our own faith leads the nation
body: Hear it, {{terms.civic.people}}! The faith we founded, {{religion}}, is now the faith of most of our cities! Light a lamp in every window, and tell the children whose prayers won the count!

variants.headline: A new majority, an old day of rest
body: The count now gives {{religion}} a majority in most of our cities, and the first place the change will be felt is the weekly calendar. Shops that have closed on the same day for generations will hear new arguments about which day is holy. A nation can share a government and still quarrel over when to rest; expect the quarrel at the counter, not in the temple.

variants.headline: {{religion}} takes most cities in {{civilization}}
body: In {{civilization}}, {{religion}} now leads in most cities, displacing {{former}}. The change is plain at the border market, where the feast-day stalls have moved to a new corner and the old ones stand half empty. Our own traders will need to learn the new calendar before they set out.

variants.headline: {{religion}} gains a majority across the border
body: In the country over the border, {{religion}} now leads in most cities, where {{former}} led at the last count. The ferrymen have begun asking passengers which feast they keep before quoting a fare. A traveler who cannot answer will be taken for a stranger, and charged like one.

variants.headline: Two prayer books for a binder in {{civilization}}
body: Letters from {{civilization}} relate that {{religion}} has gained a majority in most of its cities, where {{former}} was lately first. A binder there reports orders for two kinds of prayer book and has hired a second apprentice to keep pace. He will not say which creed pays better, only that both pay on time.

variants.headline: Border towns: ask after the feast days
body: Border towns, take note: {{religion}} now leads in most cities across the line, where {{former}} held the count before. Fairs and market days may move with the new feast. Ask before you load the cart, or you will arrive to shuttered stalls.

variants.headline: {{key}} gains a majority in {{count}} nearby cities
body: {{count|town|towns}} within reach of our border now keep {{key}} as their majority faith. In the market nearest the crossing, a copyist has taken on an apprentice to meet the demand for prayer sheets. What began in one household has become a trade.

variants.headline: The border tally of faiths
body: Faith now leading in the border towns: {{key}}
Towns that have made the change: {{count}}
Read together, the count is no longer a rumor; it is a row of neighbors.

variants.headline: The ferryman counts the towns
body: The ferryman at the crossing says he can tell the new pilgrims by their shoes. {{count|town|towns}} along the border road have taken up {{key}}, and the road to the shrine is worn bare before the feast. "Same road," he says, "more feet."

variants.headline: One town, then the field
body: One hearth keeps {{key}}: a neighbor smiles. {{count|hearth|hearths}} keep it: the street raises a shrine. One stalk bends; the whole field turns.

variants.headline: {{religion}} gains a new article of belief
body: The keepers of {{religion}} have added to the faith at home, and the first copies of the new words went to the schools. In the oldest shrine, a reader practiced the passage aloud until the children could answer it without prompting. The change is small on the page and large in the week, since every household now has one more thing to teach.

variants.headline: The state's stewardship adds to the creed
body: We are pleased to report that {{religion}} has been enriched with further observances, and that the work was done in good order. The new copies reached the shrines before the feast, and the keepers had time to learn them properly. Credit belongs to those who planned the change and to the clerks who carried it out without a single missed town.

variants.headline: The rites set in order anew
body: In this season the faith of {{religion}} was reformed by our own hand. The elders sat in the shrine hall through a long week of reading, and when they came out, one fast had been shortened and one procession moved to the morning. The people received the change quietly, as they receive weather.

variants.headline: Hear it! The national faith is deepened
body: Listen, {{terms.civic.people}}, listen! {{religion}} has grown deeper, and the new words are read in every shrine from the capital to the frontier! Learn them at home, and no stranger will know them better than you!

variants.headline: Our cities keep more than one faith
body: {{faithful}} of our cities keep {{founded}}, the faith this nation founded, while {{divided}} follow other creeds: {{others}}. In one coastal town, the two congregations draw water from the same well and have agreed to keep their feast days apart. The arrangement works, though nobody has written it down.

variants.headline: A founded faith, unevenly kept
body: A nation that founds a faith should be able to say how many of its own cities keep it. The count today is {{faithful}} for {{founded}} and {{divided}} for other creeds.
The ministry owes the public an account of what it has spent on shrines and where. Every rival creed won its ground one town at a time, and each of those towns was somebody's failure to teach.

variants.headline: Madam, on the counting of divided cities
variants.byline: A Keeper of a Small Shrine
body: Madam, your paper counts the cities that keep other creeds as though the number were a debt. On my street the two congregations share a wall and a ladder, and I have yet to see the wall complain.
Print this as well: {{founded}} is kept by people, not by tallies, and the keeper who knows both prayers is the one the neighbors call at midnight.

variants.headline: The tally of faiths in our cities
body: Cities keeping {{founded}}, the faith we founded: {{faithful}}
Cities keeping another creed: {{divided}}
Names of those creeds: {{others}}
One government over all of them, and more than one prayer beneath it.

variants.headline: {{city}} turns to {{religion}}
body: {{religion}} now holds a majority in {{city}}. At the evening meal, a father gives the old blessing and his children answer with the new one without missing a beat. Neither blessing has driven the other from the table.

variants.headline: Good news, people of {{city}}
body: People of {{city}}, the news is good! {{religion}}, the creed this nation founded, now leads in your city, and new converts are joining its congregation. Open the shutters, put out the flags, and come to the shrine on the feast day!

variants.headline: A creed not of our founding leads in {{city}}
body: {{religion}}, a creed this nation did not found, is now the majority faith of {{city}}. The recent conversions in the city have gone its way.
The shrine by the east gate still opens on the old feast, but the keeper counts fewer families each year. He has begun to lend the benches to travelers rather than see them stand empty.

variants.headline: New hymns over the wall
body: In {{city}}, neighbors say you can hear the change before you see it: singing over the wall on a morning that used to be quiet. The city's majority faith is now {{religion}}, and the singers no longer lower their voices. "They'll wake the whole street," one woman says, then hums the tune herself.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} founds a pantheon
body: {{civilization}} has raised its first pantheon. The altar was set in the open with no roof over it, and the families who came named the powers they meant to honor, one after another, until the light failed. A people with a pantheon has begun to agree on what it owes the unseen.

variants.headline: They say the first altars are ours
body: They say it from the wells to the gates: our own people have raised a pantheon at last. The elders named the old powers aloud, and the young ones stayed to hear the whole list. It is a fine season to be counted among the faithful.

variants.headline: A pantheon entered in the foreign record
body: In this year the people of {{civilization}} raised a pantheon. The record sets down the founding and the day, without judging what the rites mean or how long they will last. What that nation holds sacred is its own concern; our scribes count the worshippers and write the number.

variants.headline: Notice to travelers: a new pantheon at {{cityName}}
body: Travelers should know that {{civilization}} has founded a pantheon at {{cityName}}, and that its first teaching is called {{belief}}. The rites are open to visitors who come with courtesy. Those who prefer to pass by may do so; the road is wide enough for both.

variants.headline: This nation has founded {{religion}}
body: This nation has founded {{religion}}. The first congregation gathered in a hall lent by a merchant, and by the second evening the crowd had spilled into the yard. The new faith is ours from its first word, and its keepers are already asking where the next shrine should stand.

variants.headline: Hear it! A religion of our own
body: Hear it in the square! {{religion}} is founded, and it is ours! Let every town raise a shrine before the year turns, and let travelers hear the name on every road!

variants.headline: What a founded faith carries with it
body: The founding of {{religion}} gives this nation something it did not have before: a creed that speaks with our accent. Its first teachers are our own people, and its first prayers were said in our own towns.

That advantage will travel farther than any army. A merchant who keeps our prayers will trust our word before he trusts a stranger's, and a town that sings our hymns will hear our name in them. The faith is a road, and it runs both ways.

variants.headline: A founding entered in the record
body: The faith of {{religion}} was founded among our people in this season, and the event is entered here in the plainest terms. The first names went into the shrine book one by one as the families came forward, and the keeper read the list aloud before the lamp was put out. What the faith becomes will be set down in later years.
